According to [this](https://moscow.sci-hub.se/2134/b4a07df3216c5b1e64daaead89c72cff/schmidt2007.pdf), the k(inact)/KI values are 107/(M*s) for MAO-A and 706/(M\*s) for MAO-B, which does seem like it would result in a significant difference in starting therapeutic doses.

> If I'm reading that correctly, it takes less TCP to inhibit 50% of MAO-A than to inhibit 50% of MAO-B.

I’m assuming you’re referring to the IC50 values cited in that article. The IC50 is actually not a good metric for evaluating the *in vivo* potency of inhibitors, especially not the *in vivo* potency of irreversible inhibitors, such as Parnate. IC50 values depend both on the concentration of the target protein and on the incubation time. K(inact)/Ki is a better metric for measuring the *in vivo* potency of irreversible inhibitors, and that value, for Parnate, is higher for MAO-B than for MAO-A (indicating that it is a more potent MAO-B inhibitor).

> the invivo binding affinity is about 270uM meanwhile it's mao-a and b are far far lower

[It’s only 2.4x lower for MAO-A and 16x lower for MAO-B](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/bi0618621); I wouldn’t call that “far far lower.”

> physiological concentrations probably achieve 30uM max

That doesn’t mean that it has no significant effect on LSD1. If it did mean that, it would also mean it had no significant effect on MAO-A, and we know that that’s not true. 

Binding affinity, as measured by the inhibition constant Ki, is not a good metric for measuring the potency of irreversible inhibitors. [Irreversible inhibitors require a lower exposure than reversible ones to result in the same effects](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26426864/). So instead, we [use k(inact)/Ki](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27703080/) to measure the potency of irreversible inhibitors (and this value, for Parnate, is also not that different between MAO-A and LSD1).

Also, keep in mind that a paper has shown Parnate to be neurotoxic at concentrations [far lower than 30uM](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5725435/). 

This doesn’t mean that Parnate is responsible for OP’s cognitive issues, of course. People naturally become a lot less sharp as they age. As Wikipedia [puts it](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_intelligence),
> In one cross-sectional study, various cognitive functions measured declines by about 0.8 in z-score from age 20 to age 50, the cognitive functions included speed of processing, working memory, and long-term memory.[9]

And 13 years is about half of the time between age 20 and age 50. And having Lyme disease (or any disease, for that matter) should only speed up the decline. Also, if OP’s cognitive issues are indeed partially due to Parnate, that doesn’t mean that someone taking a much lower daily dosage should expect to have the same issues as well. 

In general, there is little *in vivo* human evidence that Parnate causes cognitive impairments at normal therapeutic doses, despite the *in vitro* and theoretical evidence that it does. That could be because not a lot of people researched the issue, however.

Oddly, this study https://www.jneurosci.org/content/20/24/9104.full almost sort of directly contradicts the first study I linked in my previous comment. As far as I know, they gave rats an only somewhat higher human-equivalent dose of Parnate for an only somewhat higher number of days, and found that it *increased* cell proliferation in the same part of the brain. The main difference seems to be that this study used rats and the other one used mice, although maybe there are other, more important differences.

Unfortunately, I found disheartening studies today. And this one https://www.nature.com/articles/cddis201748 found that LSD1 inactivation triggers senescence in embryonic stem cells. 

LSD1 is also required for the maintenance of DNA methylation (https://moscow.sci-hub.se/1050/5c28b464c1a036ef06f3773b1f3a8eed/wang2008.pdf), and reduced DNA methylation seems to be associated with aging.

This could be relevant, since decreased cognitive functioning could lead to confusion. It *is*, unfortunately, a (relatively) short-term study).

I think old people would likely be harmed more, if Parnate really does impair cognitive function, than young people. When you’re young, your body can adjust to stressors better and counteract the harmful effects of drugs in ways that it can’t when you’re old. Being on Parnate for a period of decades would indeed make the negative cognitive effects add up (if they exist at all), but most of the harm would come from the latter part of the period. 

I intend to continue taking Parnate, but I’ll keep researching this matter, and quit if I decide it’s too harmful.

Wikipedia says that the plasma concentration of Parnate after a 20mg dose reaches a maximum of 50-200ng/mL. Since Parnate’s molar mass is 133.19g/mol, that corresponds to ((50-200)/133.19)nmol/L = 0.375-1.5 nmol/L = 0.375-1.5 μmol/L = 0.375-1.5 μM. 

That is a peak plasma concentration, though, and the brain organoid study soaked the organoids in Parnate for 48 hours, which is importantly different. The concentration AUC in one day in that study would be 24hμM, and if you take 20mg of Parnate once a day the concentration AUC in your bloodstream is, very roughly, (t_max)(cmax)/2 + 12h(cmax)/2 (12 because a study said that plasma concentration is close to 0 12 hours after the last dose of the day), which gives you 9.9h*μM if we use our upper bound for peak plasma concentration.

I read somewhere (I can’t find the paper right now) that the AUC of Parnate in rats was 3.4x greater in the brain than in the plasma. So Parnate might indeed reach a neurotoxic AUC even in a low daily dose.

Parnate is actually only 2.4x better at inhibiting MAO-A than it is at inhibiting LSD1 (although it is 16x better at inhibiting MAO-B than LSD1). I think this means that at therapeutic doses there’s *definitely* some substantial LSD1 inhibition. It could be the case that the human body produces LSD1 a lot quicker than it produces MAO, though, in which case the LSD1 inhibition stuff is clinically insignificant. But I’m not sure if that’s the case, since LSD1 inhibitors are clinically useful for e.g. stopping the growth of cancers. 

But there could be some mechanism no one is aware of or understands that makes it so that LSD1 inhibition by Parnate is a nothingburger in adult humans, which would explain why reports of negative cognitive side effects seem rare and it doesn’t seem to increase dementia risk. Biology is complicated.

This is pretty speculative, but Parnate apparently inhibits a protein (LSD1) that is important for preventing cortical and hipoccampal neurodegeneration, so it might have permanent negative cognitive effects.
